benefits.rawBenefitsSummary: Esports, as a whole, is still a new industry, even more so in the Philippines. Across the board, salaries in esports are still very low, regardless of if you are in the backend, or as a talent (streamer, shoutcaster, pro player, etc). I've asked my coworkers as well as other people in the industry, and a lot, if not all of them, said that they are earning less than their previous jobs. Unless you're a big-name influencer who's caught the attention of big-name brands to sponsor you, or a famous streamer who can pull in big numbers, or a good pro player who wins big tournaments, you're not going to make a lot of money in esports. This sounds kinda salty but I'm really not. I'm glad we're all working towards a future where going into a career in esports is viable and sustainable and open for a lot of people. Behind the scenes, there're still positions like sales executives, account managers, project managers, graphic designers, photographers, videographers, video editors, audio engineers, talent managers, road managers, social media managers, writers, HR, accountants, legal, doctors, chefs, psychologists, therapists, and more; some esports organizations and companies are looking for a whole lot of people.

benefits.rawBenefitsSummary:
I was job searching even before I graduated because I didn't want to compete with thousands of new graduates in the IT-related fields. I don't think I'm that good of a software engineer yet and I'm not a good student but I do have some experience with hackathons, competitions, and funded projects etc. I had to really tailor my resume and Linkedin to get responses on my online applications. One day I received an interview invitation from a local crypto related company. 

The interview was basically just confirmations on my resume(no technical interview!!) and I got hired on the spot! I guess the company was quickly looking to fill the spot and maybe they liked what they saw on my resume.

If I have to give you a tip, I think applying for jobs even before your graduation is the key! You don't want to compete with tens of thousands of new IT graduates. And also, join competitions, do self projects, don't 100% rely on schoolwork because IT is a very competitive field. It is as competitive as it is rewarding though so, just make sure you work hard and pick the right companies not the dogshit exploitative WITCH companies here in the PH. 

The job I got is very good so far. <40 hour workweeks. No time-in time-outs, and I have an awesome team! Good luck on your search reader and may your hard work pay off!

mentorAdviceQuote:
AB 1997, LLB 2004 (another school), MBA 2010. I started working in 2004, one month before my 29th birthday and two months before my wedding day. I had a complete career shift in 2010, where I had to start from scratch (zero income). With the Lord's hand prodding me on - climbing the ladder through a combination of private and government institutions - I've managed to land at my present position. It won't be my last. 

1. If your work allows you to live life the way you want to live it while sticking to your core values then you should be happy and content. 
2. Your needs based on your life stage (i.e. single-new grad, single-thirtyish, married-no kids, married-with kids, married-with kids-double income, etc.) will determine the hierarchy of your core values.
3. Change happens. Adjust accordingly.
4. Being an Atenean gets you on the shortlist. Being a likable person (because that HR assistant and HR supervisor will most probably not be from The Ateneo) gets you the job.
5. Companies have hiring budgets. Don't worry about the pay. You're an Atenean so you will always be on the shortlist for a management position. Get in, learn everything you can, and be really good at what you do so you'll be first on that list.

mentorAdviceQuote:
[Started work 2010] - main line of work is in Retail/E-Commerce

(Believe it or not, although the salary looks big, it's still not enough for a family. Spouse also makes +100k a month.)

Some pieces of advice (I actually have so many HAHA but here's a few):

1. Be humble! especially on your first job. I started working by doing menial stuff for marketing and sales. Carried and counted inventory. Went to clients and physically demo-ed products. Arranged displays for marketing. Stood in front of crowds calling for customers. You will earn more respect from others if you do those things. I still do those things now!

2. Learn how to adapt to different people. Learn how to read their expressions and intentions. Learn how to adapt to wherever you're placed in. Learn how to do politics if necessary. These are things that take effort but will really be good for you in the long run.

3. On joining startups - remember: startups that burn money really easily (unnecessary parties, extra bonuses, unusually high salaries) but don't actually make any profits will likely fail sooner than you expect.

4. Nobody does presentations in real life the way they teach you in school. Nobody actually likes presentations, haha. It's how you communicate your message that's the most important. More than making your slides pretty, put 99% of the effort into making your message work for your audience.

5. EXCEL IS LIFE. MASTER IT NOW. Almost everything requires some form of analytics now. You can start with getting sales data and manipulating it by thinking of results-oriented questions like "How did my product category XX do in 2017? Is it enough to reach YY growth in 2018?" Something like that. Everyone will praise you for good data manipulation and interpretation skills. (DON'T GET USED TO VLOOKUP, USE INDEX(MATCH)!! IT'S MUCH SEXIER HAHA)

mentorAdviceQuote:
Most of my growth really came from handling my superior. Her reputation is quite notorious (actually 'quite' would be an understatement). Everyone evades her brand because she's moody, easily stressed and only chooses the jobs she wants to do (and the rest goes to us). As for career growth, she refused to promote her encoder of 4 years as a senior encoder because she still has to train the other new hire. Same goes for her assistants, she's known to extend their "training" before promoting them until she thinks they're "ready".  Eventually all of our main encoders resigned which then started the trend of 4 encoders (and counting) AWOLing after a week to a month in the job. 

Even though my job as an assistant is already at their junior managerial level, I still have to do a lot menial, inventory system related or clerical tasks because we dont have senior encoders. 

There are still some managerial tasks but most of my growth is hindered due to her lack of people. I've been here for almost a year now  but I dont even know how to help with Business Review reports because I've mostly been handling encoder tasks. Talking to her about tasks feels like a grill session. When I mess something up (which is common for other assistants since everything is learn on the go), the entire floor knows because she'd shout everything. She's done this to me in front of store staffs and area managers over 15 pesos withholding tax when I ordered food for our meeting.

Why didn't I leave right away? I guess I didn't notice how badly I was being treated for the first few months. I thought everyone was going through the same thing. I only started to notice when other people told me. But by that time, i was already around 6 months into the job. I didn't want my first job to only have a duration of 6 months because it would look bad. I'm almost done with my first year. Planning to resign soon because it's getting really hard to look for a new job with all the heat I'm getting from my leaves. Would've stayed if she was a good mentor, but she's not. I feel bad for leaving the team though. They're good people.

As for the good side, it's very character building. I think my skin grew a lot thicker. I can take criticism very well now. I know how to argue/fend for myself when I have to. Knowing when to adjust and let things slide. I can appear to have a cool head when I'm being presured. I know what I shouldn't be in the future. Overall, it's a humbling experience. Maybe that's what I needed.

mentorAdviceQuote:
Batch 2017. Treat your employment decisions as your own personal investments since you will be spending most of your time at work. Always be open and flexible to explore areas outside the norm. Rule of thumb is that to look for emerging or high growth industries where the talent pool is not yet as crowded, giving you more space to make a name for yourself. In the Philippines, the fintech space is still an emerging industry wherein lots of new ventures are coming out yet the talent pool locally is being derived from traditional financial institutions or tech companies not specifically involved in financial services. Make your 20s to before 30 meaningful since that stage is a pretty good launching pad for your future down the line. 

Concept of career hacking is very important - networking very well and building up your skills through self study courses such as Udemy, etc. and getting exposed to other departments of your current company will help you get a better understanding of the industry and your role in your company's business. Be open to opportunities outside the "known" companies since these guys tend to give better compensation and bigger responsibilities than bigger organizations for as long as you do sufficient due diligence in making sure that the company/start up's business is viable, sustainable, and in the right position to succeed in the future. Going back to the first part, treat it as your own personal investment. Going down this path - for as long as you do it right can help you get that compensation level (from mid xx,000 to xxx,xxx) and scope of work much faster than staying in a top corporate for x years. There are those opportunities, look for them but they will not be readily available via linkedin, social media, etc. Networking is really the key. Once you land that interview, know what you know but attitude and drive are top considerations to stand out among the rest of the applicants. Hence build yourself early up via skills and show up with a winning attitude.

mentorAdviceQuote:
FOR FRESH GRADUATES
1. Get an initial feel of the industry you are entering first, This can be achieved thru the ff:
- OJT PROGRAMS - As in legit OJT PROGRAMS wherein you actually become a part of the Host Company's daily Operations. 
(What I mean about this is by literally learning the industry/trade not just doing clerical paper work or hanging out by the XEROX machine all day long.)
- MENTOR - Look for a mentor, individuals or people who will teach you everything about the industry.
- ALWAYS LOOK FORWARD TO TRAININGS - Trainings are a good source of knowledge and actual advice from professionals in your respective industry.
- BE PATIENT - There are no shortcuts to actual success in the industry of your choosing. You will need to learn everything (the IN's & OUT's).

FOR TENURED EMPLOYEES
1. Don't stop Learning, Even if you have already reached a high position in your line of work.
- Always learn a thing or two about your profession/industry every day or every week.
2. Share what you learn to your Juniors, This allows you to train the next generation to be better and more well equipped to deal with problems they may encounter down the road of their Career.
3. Be Humble.

FOR PEOPLE LOOKING TO SWITCH CAREER TRACKS (changing lines of industry, etc.)
1. Know the industry first, Know the basics before shifting to that Work/Industry.
2. Don't be surprised but you will be starting from the bottom again. (This is true for industries that are not related to one another)

FOR OVERALL ADVISE
1. NO ONE IS PERFECT - people will make mistakes, YOU will make mistakes accept this fact as early as possible.
- This will allow you to have a much more wider field of understanding.

ADMU pre-med, other school for medicine proper. I worked a year before med school in the IT and BPO industries. Pay was okay, but the schedule was crazy and I found the work too mundane.

Decided to pursue my original plan. Got caught up in the crazy world of medicine. The first 3 years are like HS and college, stuck in lectures except the pace is way faster and the information overload takes getting used to. Your endurance will surely be tested especially by your 4th year (clerkship) and 5th year (senior internship) as you will start rotating in diff depts and doing 24-36hr (or more) duties every 3-4 days. 

I passed the boards last year, decided to take some time off to detox. Only started working again (this time as a licensed MD) at age 28. Currently doing moonlighting as a freshly minted MD in general practice. Its like freelancing for doctors where you get various jobs on fixed term basis. You're paid by the hr. Going rate for new docs/GPs is at 300-350/hr. 

You work hard, and you will reap what you sow. Work 5-6x/week and go on straight hospital duties and you can go up to 80-100k/mo. If you do more relaxed outpatient settings, you can easily earn 60k/mo and thats with regular 8 am-5 pm hrs.

Pay for doctors in the PH is not commensurate to the years of study. Resident salary (further training) is a pittance compared to moonlighting but will pay off later once you reach specialist status. Surgeons can get up to 500k and up guaranteed.

WORD OF ADVICE FOR ASPIRING DOCTORS: If medicine is really your passion, then go for it. You will be comfortable. But if you are just in it for the money, you can exert less effort and earn higher in other fields (i.e. business) :))

mentorAdviceQuote:
Don't be afraid to negotiate your salary and allowances but make sure that you do good work to show that you're worth the increase.

Make it a point to do job interviews even if you're not looking for a job for the ff reasons: 
1. Know your worth outside your company. It's normal to get annual increases of 10% but you may be surprised that your job might be worth more outside. 
2. You can use this info as an added point to your negotiation talks. Your superiors will realize your worth (if they don't see it yet) if other companies want you. 
3. Brushing up on your interview skills is always helpful. 

Find a mentor within the company. Someone who can give good testimonials especially during promotion periods. Make yourself invaluable to him or her by helping do 
 legwork. You may learn something. 

Be nice to everyone from the CEO to the janitors. People notice this. 

Be confident in speaking to superiors and to expats. If anything, they'd think about you first for cross market projects. Filipinos,  in general, are quite shy and are often looked over for these projects.

mentorAdviceQuote:
Before you reach 30 years old, always job-hop every 2-years to increase your salary worth.
You may do this job-hopping until 33 to 35, but after that age it's best to stay loyal to a company unless a better opportunity presents itself, e.g., a salary offer that is at least twice your salary at that time. 

Accept a job-hop if it could provide a salary increase of at least 40% when you're younger than 35.

Another thing: in 2010 you could only marry if you're earning at least 20k per month and, after that, it will cost you an additional 10k for each child you wish to have.  But that's for year 2010.  

For 2021, you should adjust for the yearly inflation and compute how much is 2010's 20k value today.  My back-of-the-napkin calculation says that in 2021, you need to have a monthly salary of 33k to marry and an additional 15k per child to support.

Don’t sell yourself short and acknowedge your strengths, ask and accept feedback, and always be consistent. 

Don’t be afraid to fail but make sure you learn from it and improve. Acknowledge mistakes but always have action plans. Be accountable and treat your work as a partnership with your clients, managers, and colleagues. Always think of better ways to improve your current processes and don’t hesitate to share ideas no matter how crazy it may sound at first. 

Encourage growth and always motivate yourself and your colleagues. If you are struggling or unsatisfied with your work, don’t be afraid to ask help and seek guidance - your leaders won’t know what support you need unless you tell them. 

Good luck!

When you're starting, do your best to get noticed. Once you get to mid or upper level management, you can start bullshitting your way around (at least for SMEs like mine). mentorAdviceQuote:
There's a lot of good recommendations already mentioned by previous people so I'll try not to be repetitive.
(1) Don't be afraid to ask for more (more responsibilities, salary increase, higher asking, etc. - whatever it is... if you can justify, then ask for it).
(2) Build a good resume. You're selling yourself and your resume is the first layer your audience will see. Don't just copy paste everything, take time to understand your previous responsibilities and what you contributed to each company you worked for. You can describe your role with a short blurb and focus more on highlighting your projects.
(3) Do recon before you apply / accept a job offer. 
(4) Take your vacation days.
(5) Again, know your worth. Don't be afraid to quit. Don't be afraid to job hop. As long as you have a good reason and you can explain it well, good companies wouldn't mind. Forget about your "hiya" and "utang na loob".

mentorAdviceQuote:
It is my first job so I might be needing your advice also HAHAHHA but I'll have my input here:

-Before accepting job offer, consider the mandated workweek-hours, required ba mag-OT or not, the non-taxable benefits, and the programs (trainings, loan, employee-employer relationships) they have kasi doon mo matitimbang if the compensation is good, or you might be just pesos away from being a minimum wage earner. Greatest luxury you'll ever have in a job is having those I stated above in good amount +WFH/Hybrid set-up. [Metro Manila traffic is hindi nakakaganda]

-Sa katulad kong bata pa, explore different niches until your time, skills, and health allows. Find where you're best suited and will make you advance compensation-wise, skills-wise, opportunities-wise. I'm still on this stage so I'll get the hang of it, hope me I'll be happy.

-Totoo sabi nilang choose your teammates lalo na kung starting ka pa. Those soft-skills na binabalewala natin nung College, marerealize niyo kung bakit siya important once you enter the job, ang hirap kapag nahaharap ka sa communication challenge such as different age groups, attitude bosses/teammates, work politics, lack of training/coaching/mentoring. Even if they are good, continue to hone your soft and hard-skills and be a better person both for work and for life.

Advice:

1. If you are still in school, try to learn skills while looking for opportunities to earn money as a side hustle.

3. Don't be afraid to ask for a raise that matches your skills and current workload. mentorAdviceQuote:
I used to feel small when I first started working because I didn’t come from the “big schools.” There were moments when I felt inferior - but I never settled for less, because I knew what I was capable of. Over time, I realized that your school may give you a head start, but it’s your work ethic, experience, skills, how well you collaborate, your consistency (and yes, a whole lot of grit and a bit of luck!) that truly take you places.

So to everyone who didn’t come from the big schools: don’t be scared! :)

One thing I always remember from my favorite line manager (a.k.a. my mentor) is this: ALWAYS BE VISIBLE. Not the “Jollibee” kind of visible (yung maingay lang pero walang substance), but visible in the right way. Do your job well. Step up for presentations. Engage with managers and leaders. Let your outputs speak for you. Provide feedbacks and be open to feedbacks.

I got promoted twice because of my results. I was never the loudest in the room. But the people around me will vouch for me (even without me asking) because they know what I can deliver.

One last tip: beware of office chismis. Don’t entertain it, and avoid being part of it as much as possible. It’s a rabbit hole that only breeds toxicity. It can quietly destroy everything you’re working hard to build.

Hopping: your salary jumps ahead of inflation (20% to 40% jump) vs <10% inflation

Job hopping helps your income outrun the rising cost of living

mentorAdviceQuote:
1. Stop collecting vanity metrics.

Don't chase a company name just for the prestige on your LinkedIn, and don't assume a new degree or certification is a golden ticket. Real leverage comes from finding the intersection of high scarcity and high business pain. Find the messy, complicated niche in your industry that everyone complains about but nobody wants to fix—and own it. When you become the person who directly protects or generates revenue, you get to write your own price tag based on execution, not your years of tenure.

2. Stabilize first then grow later & and take the jobs and tasks no one likes
If you have the safety net to take a massive career gamble right now, take it. But if you have a family depending on you, protect the baseline first. Do not jump into the fire. Lock down your stable 9-to-5, and build your leverage quietly in the background until your 'side' portfolio and skills is so undeniably strong that switching jobs is no longer a risk—it's a guaranteed upgrade.

mentorAdviceQuote:
I am able to double my salary with less than a year of experience in my next company due to the company's prestige and the broad scope of my work.

For your 1st job, it is ideal if you have strong ownership of your outputs (works for companies with low tech maturity), so much so that HR interviewers thought that all I work on are just my solo projects. Also, whenever an app was requested of me, I actively account for features that I think the end users will need despite it not initially requested of me. This approach works for this industry because the end goal was "digitalization" and making people's lives easier.

As for why I am moving to the next company despite my short YOE, I reached the edge of what I can learn alone, being part of a 4 member team (including our line manager). I am already considered the expert for all automation and software-side digitalization despite my entry-level status, which I take issue on because what can I learn if I'm the most 'experienced' already? This is a prelude to stagnation. Also, no one is able to validate or review my codes, apps, dashboards due to me being the only person in this role, which spells disaster to my work's reliability and quality. I do not want to adopt bad habits, and I desire teammates that push each other towards growth as well as mastery of technical skill.
